components.gap: The definition itself is complete, but the source extent for it (secs. 3.1-3.2, pp. 103-105 and 107) is only partly reported at body 89-121. Missing source items: (1) p. 107: 'The central idea is to exploit the invariant characteristics of structural equations without committing to a specific functional form.' (2) pp. 103-104: Wright's disease/symptom illustration itself is not given. This comprises eq. (1) y = beta x + u_Y, with Nature examining x and u and assigning Y; x = u_X; the rewriting (2) x = (y - u_Y)/beta, which could be misread as the symptom influencing the disease; Fig. 1; and fn. 6 (linear relations are illustrative only, with standardized variables). Body 105-115 gives only the abstract claim it illustrates. (3) p. 104: the diagram encodes the possible existence of direct influence of X on Y and the absence of influence of Y on X. The equations encode the quantitative relationships 'to be determined from the data'. Under the path-coefficient reading, a unit increase in X yields beta units of Y regardless of the other variables and regardless of 'whether the increase in X originates from external or internal influences'. Only the absent-arrow claim is reported. (4) p. 104: exogenous factors 'are responsible for variations observed in the data'. Since they often cannot be measured precisely, one 'must resign to merely acknowledging their existence and assessing qualitatively how they relate to other variables in the system'. Body 95-97 keeps only the measurement remark. (5) pp. 104-105: a possible correlation of disturbances is drawn as a dashed double arrow. Causal assumptions are encoded 'not in the links but, rather, in the missing links', and a missing double arrow claims zero covariance. Both kinds of assumption are 'causal, not associational, since none can be determined from the joint density of the observed variables'. The association between disturbances can be uncovered only in an experimental setting or from other causal assumptions. None of this is reported as the source's claim. Report each item as the source's claim and relate it to def:p16-finite-scm.

components.gap: Body 227-236 reports 'two further claims on p. 107' but omits other claims in the same sec. 3.2-3.2.2 extent. (1) p. 107: structural equation modeling 'has been the main vehicle for effect analysis in economics and the behavioral and social sciences (Goldberger, 1972; Duncan, 1975; Bollen, 1989)'. Also 'until recently, no comparable methodology has been devised' to extend it to dichotomous variables or nonlinear dependencies. (2) p. 107: the intervention-based extension 'has led to new ways of defining and estimating causal effects in nonlinear and nonparametric models (that is, models in which the functional form of the equations is unknown)'. (3) pp. 107-108: invariance 'permits us to use structural equations as a basis for modeling causal effects and counterfactuals'. Body 120-121 reports only the equation-replacement half. (4) sec. 3.2.2, p. 110: applying the replacement derivation to the linear models of Fig. 1 gives E(Y|do(x0)) = beta x0 (eq. 14). Five source claims are absent: (a) this derivation proves beta to be an effect coefficient rather than interpreting it as one; (b) beta keeps that meaning however X is selected (through f_X); (c) it also keeps it whether or not U_X and U_Y are correlated; (d) such correlations only impede estimating beta from nonexperimental data; (e) structural equations 'say absolutely nothing about the conditional expectation E(Y|X=x)', the two agreeing only under special circumstances such as cov(X,U_Y)=0, as in eq. (13). Report these as the source's claims and relate them to the finite definition, including the conditioning/replacement contrast at body 257-262.

components.gap: The source variant of this result is not preserved. Sec. 3.2.3, p. 110 is the page body 275-277 cites for 'Markovian'. There the source states that 'all causal effects are identifiable whenever the model is Markovian'. It also states that non-Markovian models, 'such as those involving correlated errors (resulting from unmeasured confounders), permit identification only under certain conditions, and these conditions too can be determined from the graph structure (Section 3.3)'. The end of sec. 3.2.2 (p. 110) adds that, since graphs encode all the information that nonparametric structural equations represent, they should permit one to solve the identification problem without algebraic analysis. None of these claims is reported. thm:p16-causal-positive-identification (body 509-525) adds full observation and full positive support. It does not say that it is the finite counterpart of the source's unqualified claim. It does not say that the source leaves observation of all variables and positivity implicit. It does not connect the need for positivity to item 2 of thm:p16-causal-nonidentification.

components.gap: (1) p. 109: body 568-569 reports only that Pearl compares the second assumption with the orthogonality condition Cov(X,U_Y)=0. It omits the normative rest of that sentence: the condition 'has been used routinely, often thoughtlessly, to justify the estimation of structural coefficients by regression techniques'. (2) Body 561-566 says the source observes that the derivation of (11)-(13) 'and likewise of P(y|do(x))=P(y|x)' uses only the two assumptions. The source ties the two assumptions to the derivation of (13) only. Of P(y|do(x))=P(y|x) it says just that it follows by 'a similar derivation, though somewhat more involved'. The extension is the handbook's own (proved in thm:p15-w02c-p15-009-chain-weak) and must not be attributed to the source. (3) p. 111: the source's conclusions from the chain calculation are not reported. One is that the model's causal assumptions let one predict the post-intervention distribution from the pre-intervention one, 'which further permits us to estimate the causal effect of X on Y from nonexperimental data, since P(y|x0) is estimable from such data'. The other is that 'we have made no assumption whatsoever on the form of the equations or the distribution of the error terms; it is the structure of the graph alone (specifically, the identity of X's parents) that permits the derivation to go through'. Body 543-545 states only the handbook's sufficient hypotheses and does not report or qualify these claims. (4) p. 107: the source illustrates the chain equations (5) by noting that the absence of Z from the arguments of f_Y 'conveys the empirical claim that variations in Z will leave Y unchanged, as long as variables U_Y, and X remain constant'. This illustration is not given. Nothing in the finite chain states this held-fixed reading of a missing argument.
